questions.stem: A cyclist covers $240$ m in $30$ s at a steady speed. Calculate her speed.
questions.modelAnswer: Speed is distance divided by time: $v = \dfrac{s}{t} = \dfrac{240}{30} = 8\text{ m/s}$.

questions.stem: A bag of flour has a mass of $12$ kg. Calculate its weight. Take $g = 9.8\text{ N/kg}$.
questions.modelAnswer: Weight is mass times gravitational field strength: $W = mg = 12 \times 9.8 = 117.6\text{ N}$, which rounds to about $118\text{ N}$.

questions.stem: A lamp has a p.d. of $6\text{ V}$ across it and carries a current of $0.25\text{ A}$. Calculate its resistance.
questions.modelAnswer: Resistance is p.d. divided by current: $R = \dfrac{V}{I} = \dfrac{6}{0.25} = 24\ \Omega$.

questions.stem: A bimetallic strip is made of brass and steel bonded together. When heated, the strip bends. Explain why it bends, state which way it bends, and give one practical use of a bimetallic strip.
markscheme: B1: brass expands more than steel for the same temperature rise (different rates of thermal expansion)
B1: the strip bends with brass on the outside of the curve (towards the steel side)
B1: any one valid use, e.g. thermostat, temperature switch, fire alarm
questions.modelAnswer: Brass and steel expand by different amounts when heated: brass expands more than steel for the same temperature rise. Because the two metals are bonded, this difference forces the strip to curve, with the more-expanding brass on the outside of the bend. This bending is used to open or close a contact in a thermostat, so heaters switch off at a set temperature.

questions.stem: An object stands $4\text{ m}$ in front of a plane mirror. State how far behind the mirror its image is formed, and give one other property of the image.
markscheme: B1: image is $4\text{ m}$ behind the mirror
B1: any one of: virtual, same size as the object, laterally inverted, upright
questions.modelAnswer: In a plane mirror the image is as far behind the mirror as the object is in front, so the image forms $4\text{ m}$ behind the mirror. The image is also virtual (no light actually passes through it), the same size as the object, and laterally inverted.

questions.stem: A train travels at a constant speed of $15\text{ m/s}$ for $20$ s. Using a speed–time graph, show how the distance travelled is found and calculate it.
markscheme: M1: states that distance is the area under a speed–time graph
questions.modelAnswer: On a speed–time graph the distance travelled equals the area between the line and the time axis. Here that area is a rectangle of height $15\text{ m/s}$ and width $20\text{ s}$, so distance $= 15 \times 20 = 300\text{ m}$.

questions.stem: A crane lifts a load of weight $500\text{ N}$ through a height of $8\text{ m}$ in $20$ s. Calculate the work done on the load and the useful power output of the crane.
markscheme: A1: $W = 4000\text{ J}$ and $P = 200\text{ W}$ (both correct with units)
questions.modelAnswer: Work done $= F \times d = 500 \times 8 = 4000\text{ J}$. Power is work done per unit time: $P = \dfrac{W}{t} = \dfrac{4000}{20} = 200\text{ W}$.

questions.stem: A force of $800\text{ N}$ acts on an area of $0.02\text{ m}^2$. Calculate the pressure. Then state how the pressure changes if the same force acts on twice the area.
markscheme: B1: doubling the area halves the pressure (to $20\,000\text{ Pa}$)
questions.modelAnswer: Pressure $= \dfrac{F}{A} = \dfrac{800}{0.02} = 40\,000\text{ Pa}$. Pressure is inversely proportional to area for a fixed force, so doubling the area to $0.04\text{ m}^2$ halves the pressure to $20\,000\text{ Pa}$.
